title: "Data sources"
pagetitle: "Data sources"
---

Every number this package hands you came from somewhere, and the somewhere matters: sources disagree, cover different countries, update on different schedules and come on different terms. This page is the comparison — what each source is good at, where it falls down, and which one to reach for.

Much of the boundary and raster material here is adapted from [`laser-init`](https://github.com/laser-base/laser-init)'s `docs/datasources.md`, which accumulated it the hard way.

For the legally operative attribution and license text, see [NOTICE.md](https://github.com/starsimhub/starsim_data/blob/main/NOTICE.md). Every dataset also carries its own attribution as data: `ssd.provenance(which)`, or `df.attrs['provenance']` on anything `load()` or `fetch()` returns.

## What comes from where

| Data | Source | Tier | How you get it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Births, deaths, migration, population | UN WPP 2024 | 0 — bundled | `load()` |
| Contact matrices | Prem 2017 / Prem 2021 / Mistry 2021 | 0 — bundled | `load()` |
| Node table: centroids, areas, p-codes | UNOCHA COD-AB, geoBoundaries | 0 — bundled | `load_nodes()` |
| Annual series, life tables, other variants | UN WPP 2024 bulk files | 2 — fetched | `fetch()` |
| Administrative boundaries with geometry | UNOCHA, geoBoundaries, GADM | 2 — fetched | `fetch_shapes()` |
| Gridded population | WorldPop | 2 — fetched | `fetch_raster()`, `fetch_nodes()` |

Tier 0 is inside the wheel: no network, byte-identical for everyone on the same version. Tier 2 is downloaded on demand and cached, because it is too big to bundle. The tier boundary is drawn by size, not by subject — which is why the *same* UN WPP release appears in both rows.

---

## Demographics

### UN World Population Prospects

**Provider:** UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs, Population Division · [population.un.org/wpp](https://population.un.org/wpp/) · CC BY 3.0 IGO

The authoritative national demographic series: all countries, 1950–2100, revised every two years.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Coverage** | 187 countries (plus aggregates this package drops) |
| **Levels** | National only — WPP has no subnational dimension at all |
| **Variants** | Medium (bundled), plus High, Low, Constant fertility and others via `fetch()` |
| **Update** | Biennial: 2022, 2024, … |

**Strengths.** Authoritative and standardised across every country, which makes cross-country comparison meaningful. Long time series with consistent methodology. Well-documented, and revised often enough to stay current.

**Limitations.** National only — if you need province-level birth rates, WPP cannot help and no amount of processing will change that. Projections are scenarios, not predictions. Estimates move between revisions, sometimes materially: a country's history can be rewritten by a new census, which is why this package versions the data by revision (`load(..., revision=2024)`) rather than silently replacing it.

**Two access routes, and why both exist.** The bundled store is built at release time from the WPP Data Portal API, filtered to decadal years and this package's countries, and frozen. That is what `load()` reads: instant, offline, ~3 MB. `fetch()` reads the UN's public bulk CSVs instead — annual resolution, complete life tables, other variants — at the cost of a 17–290 MB download. The Data Portal API needs a free Bearer token; the bulk files do not, which is why `fetch()` uses the bulk files and only the build scripts use the API.

**Watch out for.** Namibia's ISO-2 code is the string `NA`, which pandas reads as "missing" unless you pass `keep_default_na=False`. This silently dropped Namibia from every series in this package until version 0.3.0. If you process WPP CSVs yourself, this will bite you too.

## Contact matrices

Three sources, none of which supersedes the others: they differ in age resolution and country coverage, and to a lesser extent in method.

| Source | Matrix | Age bins | Countries | License |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `prem2017` | 16×16 | 5-year, 0–75+ | 152 | GPL-3.0 |
| `prem2021` | 16×16 | 5-year, 0–75+ | 177 | GPL-3.0 |
| `mistry2021` | 85×85 | single-year, 0–84+ | 36 | Apache-2.0 |

**Prem et al. 2017 and 2021** project contact patterns onto countries without their own survey, using household composition and demographic structure. 2021 is the update — more countries, revised method, and a comparison with empirical data — so prefer it unless you are reproducing older work. Both give the same five settings: `all`, `home`, `work`, `school`, `community`.

**Mistry et al. 2021** is a different trade: far finer age resolution (single years to 84) for far fewer countries (36). Use it when the age structure of transmission matters at a finer grain than five-year bins — school-entry effects, single-year cohorts — and accept the coverage limit.

Not every country appears in every source: check with `list_locations('prem2021')`. These were adapted from [epydemix-data](https://github.com/epistorm/epydemix-data), trimmed to national level; epydemix has subnational matrices this package does not include.

## Administrative boundaries

The three boundary sources are genuinely complementary, which is why all three are here and why `fetch_shapes()` has a fallback chain rather than a default.

### UNOCHA COD-AB

**Provider:** UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs · via the [laser-base mirror](https://github.com/laser-base/unocha) · CC BY 3.0 IGO

| | |
|---|---|
| **Coverage** | ~110 countries, weighted towards humanitarian operations |
| **Levels** | 0–4, varying by country |
| **Format** | Per-country zstd-compressed GeoPackage, 0.2–5 MB |
| **Key** | **P-code** |

**Strengths.** The p-codes are the reason this is the default. A p-code is the identifier that essentially all subnational humanitarian and health data is keyed on — surveillance line lists, campaign coverage, HDX datasets — so boundaries carrying p-codes join to real data, and boundaries carrying a source-specific ID do not. The boundaries themselves are usually the official government ones, vetted through UN operations, and they are updated quickly during a response.

**Limitations.** Coverage is the catch: about 110 countries, skewed towards crisis-affected ones. Stable middle- and high-income countries are often absent.

**On the global fallback.** UNOCHA also publishes a single global geodatabase on HDX, 1–2 GB, which `laser-init` falls back to when a country is missing. This package deliberately does not: a 1–2 GB download triggered implicitly by a library call is user-hostile, and geoBoundaries covers the same gap for a few MB. If you need it, download it yourself and read it with geopandas.

### geoBoundaries

**Provider:** William & Mary geoLab · [geoboundaries.org](https://www.geoboundaries.org) · CC BY 4.0

| | |
|---|---|
| **Coverage** | Near-universal (~200 countries) |
| **Levels** | 0–5, varying by country |
| **Format** | Per-country zip, 1–50 MB; plus global CGAZ GeoPackages |
| **Key** | `shapeID` (not a p-code) |

**Strengths.** The coverage gap-filler, and the reproducibility choice: releases are tagged, so pinning a version pins the boundaries. This package pins **v6.0.0**. The peer-reviewed methodology is documented, and the global CGAZ composites make a worldwide build one download instead of two hundred.

**Limitations.** Quality varies by country and level more than GADM's does. Identifiers are geoBoundaries `shapeID`s, so subnational data keyed on p-codes will not join without a crosswalk. Annual releases lag recent boundary changes.

### GADM

**Provider:** Global Administrative Areas · [gadm.org](https://gadm.org) · **non-commercial use only**

| | |
|---|---|
| **Coverage** | Universal |
| **Levels** | 0–5, the deepest hierarchies of the three |
| **Format** | Per-country GeoPackage with every level in one file, 1–100 MB |
| **Key** | `GID_n` |

**Strengths.** The most complete and most detailed of the three, with names in multiple languages and frequent updates.

**The license is the constraint.** GADM is free for non-commercial use only. That makes it unusable in a lot of applied public-health work, and it means this package can fetch it for you but can never redistribute anything derived from it. Two consequences you should know about:

- GADM is **not** in the automatic fallback chain. `fetch_shapes(..., source='gadm')` has to be asked for by name, and prints a reminder about the terms.
- The bundled node table is **not** built from GADM, and the build script refuses to be. The constraint is recorded as data on the source descriptor (`ShapeSource.redistributable`), not as a comment someone might not read.

### Choosing between them

`fetch_shapes()` with no `source=` tries UNOCHA, then geoBoundaries. That default is right for most disease modelling: p-codes where they exist, coverage everywhere else. Override it when:

- **you need level 4–5** — geoBoundaries or GADM;
- **you are reproducing a published analysis** — whichever it used, pinned;
- **you need a specific country's official boundaries** — check all three against the national statistical office, they do disagree;
- **you are joining to p-coded data** — UNOCHA, and if UNOCHA lacks the country you need a crosswalk rather than a substitute.

One thing to be careful about: the three sources do not always agree on *how many* units a country has, or where the lines run. Mixing sources across countries in one analysis is usually fine; mixing them across years for the same country is usually not. The node table records `source` per row for exactly this reason.

## Gridded population

### WorldPop

**Provider:** WorldPop, University of Southampton · [worldpop.org](https://www.worldpop.org) · CC BY 4.0

| | |
|---|---|
| **Coverage** | Global, with gaps for very small territories |
| **Resolution** | 1 km (this package); 100 m available upstream |
| **Years** | 2000–2030 across two product series |
| **Format** | GeoTIFF, 1–40 MB per country-year |
| **Method** | Random-forest disaggregation of census counts |

This is what turns a boundary file into a metapopulation: sum the grid inside each polygon and you have a population per node. `fetch_nodes()` does exactly that.

**Strengths.** Global, open, fine-grained, UN-adjusted, and extensively validated. The time series lets you age a model's spatial population structure rather than holding it fixed.

**Limitations, and one that matters.** These are *modelled* estimates, not counts. The constrained product used here will not equal the UN WPP national total for the same year — for Kenya 2020 it comes out about 1.2% low. Neither number is wrong; they are answering slightly different questions. If your model needs the national total to match WPP, `rescale_to_national()` makes that choice explicit rather than leaving two totals silently in play. Accuracy is also better in urban than rural areas, and no uncertainty estimates ship with the standard products.

**Also.** WorldPop's server is slow — expect around 0.3 MB/s — so the first fetch for a country takes a while and later ones come from cache. Very small territories return an empty file rather than a 404; this package detects that and raises rather than handing you a corrupt raster.

---

## Reproducibility

Data sources move. Four things keep an analysis reproducible against that:

1. **Pin the package version.** Everything in tier 0 is byte-identical for a given `starsim_data` version, so `pip install starsim_data==0.4.0` pins the demographics, the contact matrices and the node table together.
2. **Pin the revision, not just the version.** `load(..., revision=2024)` fixes the WPP release explicitly, so a future rebuild that adds WPP 2026 does not change data already in use.
3. **Keep the provenance.** Every frame carries `.attrs['provenance']` — source, URL, license, citation, build timestamp and git SHA. Cached downloads get a sidecar with the URL, timestamp, size and SHA-256. Record it alongside your results; `ssd.cache_info()` shows what a run actually used.
4. **Say which boundary source you used.** It is in `nodes.source` and in the shapes' provenance. Two analyses of the same country with different boundary sources are not comparable, and the only way to notice is to have written it down.

---

## Not included

Deliberate omissions, so you know to look elsewhere rather than assume they are missing by oversight:

- **Subnational demographics.** WPP has none. National statistical offices, DHS and IPUMS are the usual routes.
- **Age-specific fertility and migration.** WPP publishes crude national rates only for these.
- **Other population rasters** — LandScan, GHSL, GRID3, Meta HRSL. WorldPop was chosen for openness and global consistency; the others are better for particular questions.
- **OpenStreetMap and Natural Earth boundaries.** OSM is community-maintained and excellent in places, unreliable in others; Natural Earth is simplified for cartography rather than analysis.
- **Health-system, mobility and climate data.** Out of scope for this package.
